lessons.title: Your First Salary: A Simple Plan
lessons.summary: Understand what actually reaches your bank account each month and set up a simple plan for your first salary. You will learn to build an emergency fund first and automate saving so it happens without willpower.

sections.heading: CTC is not what lands in your account
sections.body:
Offer letters in India usually quote CTC, or cost to company. It is everything the employer spends on you in a year, not the amount you will receive every month. CTC often includes the employer's provident fund contribution, a gratuity provision, insurance premiums and variable pay or a bonus that is paid later and only if targets are met.

From the fixed monthly part, further amounts are deducted before your salary is credited: your own PF contribution, professional tax in many states, and income tax if your income is taxable. What remains is your in-hand or take-home salary.

For example, a ₹6 lakh CTC works out to ₹50,000 a month on paper, but the monthly credit will be lower, and lower still if part of that CTC is variable pay. Ask HR for the salary breakup and plan only on the in-hand figure. Treat a bonus as a pleasant surprise, not as part of your monthly budget.
do: Ask HR for the monthly salary breakup
Plan your budget on in-hand pay only
dont: Divide CTC by 12 and assume that is your salary
Spend a bonus before it is actually paid

sections.heading: Build an emergency fund before anything else
sections.body:
An emergency fund is money kept aside only for real surprises: a job loss, a medical bill not fully covered by insurance, an urgent trip home or a broken laptop you need for work. Without it, the first surprise usually goes on a credit card or a quick loan, and the debt then eats into every later month.

A common target is three to six months of essential expenses such as rent, food, travel, phone and EMIs. For example, if your essentials cost ₹20,000 a month, three months is ₹60,000. That can feel huge in your first year, so start smaller: one month first, then build up.

Keep this money separate from your spending account, easy to access within a day or two, and in a place where its value does not swing up and down. The aim here is safety and access, not high returns.
do: Start with one month of essentials, then grow it
Keep the fund in a separate account
dont: Treat a sale or a trip as an emergency
Put emergency money where its value can fall sharply

sections.heading: Pay yourself first and automate it
sections.body:
Most people save whatever is left at the end of the month, and usually very little is left. Flip the order: decide a savings amount and move it out on salary day, before spending starts. This is often called paying yourself first.

The easiest way is a standing instruction or auto-transfer scheduled for the day after salary credit. For example, Priya, who takes home ₹38,000 in Pune, sets up an automatic ₹6,000 transfer to her emergency fund account on the 2nd of every month. She does not have to remember or feel tempted, because the money has already moved.

Start with an amount that does not hurt too much, even ₹2,000. Each time your salary rises, raise the transfer before you get used to spending the increase.
do: Schedule savings for the day after payday
Increase the transfer with every hike
dont: Wait to save until the month ends

sections.heading: A simple first-salary checklist
sections.body:
Your first few salaries set habits that are hard to change later, so keep the plan simple. Note your in-hand pay and your fixed monthly costs. Decide a savings amount and automate it. Keep a small fun budget so the plan feels realistic rather than strict.

It is normal and kind to want to give something to your parents or treat your family from your first salary. Decide the amount in advance so it comes from the plan rather than straining the month.

Also check the basics: your PF account number (UAN) is active, you know how your employer's health insurance works, and you have nominations in place where your accounts allow it. If you are unsure about tax declarations or which regime suits you, ask HR or a qualified professional, because tax rules change and depend on your situation.
do: Budget a gift for your family into the plan
Check your UAN and health cover details
dont: Copy a friend's plan without checking your own costs

takeaways: Plan on in-hand salary, not CTC.
Build an emergency fund of three to six months of essentials, starting with one.
Keep emergency money separate, safe and easy to access.
Pay yourself first by automating savings on salary day.
Raise your savings every time your salary rises.
quiz: Your offer letter says ₹7.2 lakh CTC. What should you budget with?
₹60,000 a month, which is the CTC divided by 12 months
The in-hand amount shown in your salary breakup
CTC plus the expected bonus, divided by 12
Whatever your seniors say they take home
CTC includes employer contributions and variable pay; only in-hand pay reaches your account monthly.
Which of these is the best use of an emergency fund?
A festive sale on a phone you have wanted for months
A friend's destination wedding
A hospital bill not fully covered by insurance
Booking a concert before tickets sell out
Emergency money is for real, unplanned needs, not wants that feel urgent.
Your essential monthly expenses are ₹18,000. What is a three-month emergency fund?
Where does an emergency fund belong, conceptually?
Somewhere with the highest possible returns, whatever the risk
In your daily spending account so it is handy
Lent to a friend who promises to pay it back
Somewhere separate, stable and accessible within a day or two
Safety and access matter more than returns for money you may need suddenly.
What does "pay yourself first" mean?
Buying yourself a reward on salary day as motivation to keep working
Moving your savings out on payday, before you start spending
Paying all bills before rent
Asking for an advance on your salary
Saving first, by automating it, makes it happen regardless of how the month goes.
Kunal's salary rises by ₹5,000 a month. Which step best protects his saving habit?
Raise his auto-transfer before the new pay arrives
Wait a few months to see how he spends it
Upgrade his phone on EMI since he can now afford it
Save only if money is left at the month end
Increasing savings immediately stops lifestyle spending from absorbing the whole raise.
Part of your CTC is a performance bonus paid once a year. How should you treat it?
As part of your monthly spending money
As a reason to take a bigger personal loan
As uncertain extra, not monthly budget
As already earned from day one
Variable pay depends on performance and timing, so it should not fund fixed monthly costs.
You want to give your parents ₹5,000 from each salary. What is the most sensible approach?
Give whatever happens to be left over at the end of each month
Skip it until your emergency fund is fully built
Borrow on a credit card to give more
Include it as a planned line in your monthly budget
Planning the amount lets you be generous without straining the rest of the month.
Which is the realistic first goal for a fresher who has no savings yet?
Six months of expenses within the first month
One month of essential expenses, built up steadily
Investing everything in the market straight away
Saving nothing until the salary doubles, then saving a large share
A small, reachable first target builds the habit and gives a basic cushion.
You are unsure which tax option to choose in your declaration to HR. What should you do?
Check with HR or a qualified professional
Pick whatever your batchmates picked
Ignore it, since tax never applies to freshers
Follow a video posted several years ago
Tax rules change and depend on individual income, so check with a reliable, current source.

scenarios.title: The first credit
scenarios.situation: Your first salary of ₹42,000 has just landed in your account in Hyderabad. Friends are planning a weekend trip costing about ₹12,000 each, and you also want to start saving. You have no savings yet.

options.text: Set up a ₹5,000 auto-transfer to a separate account for emergencies, pay fixed costs, then decide if the trip fits what is left.
options.feedback: Saving first and then checking affordability lets you enjoy life without starting your career in debt.

options.text: Go on the trip and start saving from next month.
options.feedback: One trip is not a disaster, but delaying the habit makes it easier to keep delaying.

options.text: Go on the trip and put it on a credit card to be paid later.
options.feedback: Starting with debt on a want means next month's salary is already partly spent.

options.text: Skip all fun for a year and save everything beyond rent and food.
options.feedback: Plans that are too strict usually collapse; a small fun budget makes saving sustainable.

scenarios.title: The CTC surprise
scenarios.situation: You accepted an offer of ₹8 lakh CTC and expected about ₹67,000 a month. Your first payslip shows a much smaller credit. You have already signed a rent agreement for ₹22,000 a month in Bengaluru.

options.text: Read the payslip line by line, ask HR to explain anything unclear, and rebuild your budget on the actual in-hand amount.
options.feedback: Understanding the deductions and budgeting on real take-home pay is the only plan that will hold.

options.text: Assume the payroll team made a mistake and complain to your manager.
options.feedback: Gaps between CTC and in-hand pay are normal; check the breakup before escalating.

options.text: Cut your savings to zero for now to cover the rent.
options.feedback: It is honest about the shortfall, but even a small automated saving keeps the habit alive while you adjust.

scenarios.title: Emergency or want?
scenarios.situation: You have built ₹45,000 in your emergency fund over eight months. Your phone screen cracks; it still works but is annoying. A new phone you like is ₹40,000 in a sale this week.

options.text: Use the emergency fund for the new phone, since it is technically a phone problem.
options.feedback: This is a want with a deadline, not an emergency; it would wipe out your safety cushion.

options.text: Get the screen repaired if needed, and start a separate monthly goal for a new phone.
options.feedback: It solves the real problem cheaply and turns the want into a planned purchase.

options.text: Live with the crack and keep saving as before.
options.feedback: It protects the fund, but planning for the upgrade avoids a later impulse buy.

cards.title: Your first salary, sorted
cards.text: The first few salaries shape your money habits for years. In two minutes, learn three moves: know your real pay, build a safety cushion, and save on autopilot.

cards.title: CTC is not your salary
cards.text: CTC includes employer PF, gratuity and variable pay. Deductions come before the credit. Budget on in-hand pay only.
cards.bad: ₹6 lakh CTC means ₹50,000 a month to spend.
cards.good: My payslip shows what is credited. I'll plan on that.

cards.title: Emergency fund comes first
cards.text: Aim for three to six months of essentials, kept separate, stable and easy to reach. Start with one month.
cards.example: For example: essentials ₹20,000 a month → three months = ₹60,000.

cards.title: Pay yourself first
cards.text: Saving whatever is left usually means saving nothing. Move savings out on payday.
cards.bad: I'll save whatever is left at the end of the month.
cards.good: Auto-transfer ₹6,000 to my savings account on the 2nd, every month.

cards.title: Emergency or just urgent?
cards.text: A sale ending soon is not an emergency. Job loss, medical bills and urgent travel are.
cards.bad: The phone sale ends Sunday. I'll use the emergency fund.
cards.good: I'll start a separate monthly goal for the phone.

cards.text: Your first-salary plan in five lines:

lessons.title: Budgeting That Actually Works
lessons.summary: Set up a simple budget you can actually stick to, using a split like 50/30/20 as a starting point. You will learn to spot where small UPI payments leak money and plan for yearly expenses before they surprise you.

sections.heading: Start with a simple split, then adjust
sections.body:
A budget is just a plan for where your money goes before the month begins. A popular starting point is the 50/30/20 split: about 50% of take-home pay for needs, 30% for wants and 20% for savings and debt repayment.

For example, on an in-hand salary of ₹40,000, that is ₹20,000 for needs such as rent, groceries, commute and phone; ₹12,000 for wants such as eating out, shopping and subscriptions; and ₹8,000 for savings.

Treat these numbers as a starting point, not a rule. If you share a flat in Mumbai, needs may take 60% and you might settle for 60/20/20. If you live with your parents, you may be able to save far more than 20%. The useful part is the habit of deciding in advance, not hitting exact percentages.
do: Adjust the split to your city and situation
Decide the savings amount first
dont: Give up because your numbers do not match 50/30/20 exactly

sections.heading: Needs, wants and the grey areas
sections.body:
Sorting spending into needs and wants sounds easy until you meet the grey areas. A phone plan is a need; the most expensive plan may not be. Getting to office is a need; a cab every day instead of the metro is partly a want.

A practical test: ask what the basic version costs. Count that as a need and the extra as a want. This is not about guilt. Wants are a planned part of the budget, and enjoying them is fine as long as they fit inside their share.

Write down your fixed needs first, because they are hardest to change: rent, EMIs, insurance, family support and commute. If they already take most of your pay, that is important information about your next rent or your next loan decision.
do: Count the basic version as a need and the upgrade as a want
List fixed costs before anything else
dont: Label every expense a need to avoid cutting it

sections.heading: Watch the UPI leak
sections.body:
UPI has made paying effortless, and that is exactly why small spends slip past. ₹40 for chai, ₹120 for a snack delivery, ₹199 for a subscription: none feels like much. But for example, ₹150 a day adds up to about ₹4,500 a month, which may be more than your monthly savings target.

Once a week, spend five minutes scrolling through your UPI and bank history. Do not judge, just notice. Most people find two or three patterns they did not realise, such as late-night food orders or subscriptions they forgot to cancel.

Some people find it helps to keep a separate account for day-to-day UPI spending and move only their wants budget into it each month. When it runs low, the month's wants are done.
do: Review your UPI history once a week
Cancel subscriptions you have not used in a month
dont: Ignore small payments because each one feels tiny

sections.heading: Plan for the expenses that are not monthly
sections.body:
Many budgets fail not because of daily spending but because of yearly or occasional costs: Diwali gifts, a wedding in the family, insurance premiums, a laptop repair or the security deposit for a new flat. They are predictable, but they arrive in lumps.

The fix is to divide them across the year. For example, if you expect to spend ₹18,000 on festivals and gifts every year, set aside ₹1,500 a month for it. When October comes, the money is ready and your regular budget is untouched.

Keep the budget itself simple: a notes app, a spreadsheet or a notebook all work. Review it monthly, and if one category keeps overflowing, change the plan rather than blaming yourself. A budget you adjust is better than a perfect one you abandon.
do: Divide yearly costs into monthly amounts
Review and adjust the budget every month
dont: Treat festivals and premiums as surprises every year

takeaways: Use 50/30/20 as a starting point and adjust it to your life.
Count the basic version as a need and the upgrade as a want.
Review UPI and bank history weekly to catch small leaks.
Turn yearly costs into a monthly set-aside.
Adjust a budget that is not working instead of abandoning it.
quiz: Your take-home pay is ₹50,000. Under a 50/30/20 split, how much goes to savings?
Rent in your city takes 40% of your pay. What is the most sensible budgeting response?
Abandon budgeting because 50/30/20 cannot work
Adjust the split, say to 60/20/20
Stop saving until your salary rises
Borrow every month to keep wants at 30%
Frameworks are a starting point; adjusting them to reality keeps the habit going.
You take a cab to office daily, though the metro works. How should you classify it?
The metro fare is a need; the extra cab cost is a want
Entirely a need, because you must get to work on time every day
Entirely a want
It does not belong in a budget
Counting the basic version as a need makes the trade-off visible without guilt.
Which habit best catches small UPI leaks?
Deleting all payment apps
Checking your account balance once a year before filing returns
Only paying in cash
A five-minute weekly review of UPI and bank history
Regular, quick reviews reveal patterns that single small payments hide.
For example, you spend ₹150 a day on small UPI payments. Roughly how much is that in a 30-day month?
You expect to spend ₹24,000 on festivals and gifts each year. What is a good monthly set-aside?
Your food-delivery budget overflows three months in a row. What is the best response?
Feel guilty and promise to try harder
Stop tracking because it is depressing
Study the pattern and adjust the plan or the habit
Use a credit card to cover the difference
Budgets should change with evidence; repeated overflow means the plan needs adjusting.
Which expense should you list first when building a budget?
Weekend outings
Items on your shopping wishlist for the next big online sale
Streaming subscriptions
Fixed costs such as rent, EMIs and family support
Fixed costs are hardest to change, so they define how much is left for everything else.
What does a separate day-to-day spending account help with?
It earns higher interest than a savings account
It caps wants at what you move in
It improves your credit score
It hides spending from your family
When only the wants budget sits in that account, running low is a clear signal to stop.
Which statement about budgeting is most accurate?
An adjusted simple budget beats an abandoned perfect one
A budget only works with expensive software
Budgets are mainly useful for people on low incomes who have no other choice
Wants should be zero in a good budget
Consistency matters more than precision or tools.

scenarios.title: The shared flat
scenarios.situation: You take home ₹35,000 in Mumbai. Your share of rent and bills is ₹16,000, commute and food cost another ₹9,000, and you have read that you should save 20%. The numbers do not seem to work.

options.text: Accept that needs take about 70% for now, save a smaller fixed amount like ₹3,500, and revisit when your pay or rent changes.
options.feedback: Adapting the framework keeps the habit alive and is honest about your costs.

options.text: Force 20% savings by putting wants on a credit card.
options.feedback: Saving while building card debt usually costs more in interest than it saves.

options.text: Skip saving until you get a raise.
options.feedback: Waiting delays the habit; even a small automated amount matters.

options.text: Look for a cheaper flat-share when the lease ends and save what you can meanwhile.
options.feedback: Sensible long-term, but it should come with a small saving amount starting now.

scenarios.title: Where did it go?
scenarios.situation: It is the 22nd and you have ₹3,000 left, though you budgeted carefully. You cannot remember any big purchase. Your UPI app shows dozens of payments this month.

options.text: Scroll through the month's payments, group them roughly and spot the two or three patterns behind the gap.
options.feedback: Looking at real data reveals small, repeated spends that memory misses.

options.text: Decide budgeting does not work for you.
options.feedback: The budget did its job by showing a problem; the next step is understanding it.

options.text: Cut all spending to zero until the 1st.
options.feedback: It protects this month, but without finding the cause the same thing will happen next month.

scenarios.title: The October crunch
scenarios.situation: Every year around Diwali you spend about ₹20,000 on gifts, travel and clothes, and every year it upsets your budget. It is now February.

options.text: Start setting aside about ₹2,500 a month in a separate goal so the money is ready by October.
options.feedback: Eight months × ₹2,500 = ₹20,000; a predictable cost becomes a planned one.

options.text: Plan to use a no-cost EMI offer in October.
options.feedback: It spreads the cost but adds future obligations, and offers can hide fees.

options.text: Promise yourself to spend less this Diwali.
options.feedback: Spending less may help, but without setting money aside the lump still hits one month.

cards.good: Metro fare is a need. The extra cab cost comes from my wants.

cards.title: Plug the UPI leak
cards.text: Small payments feel invisible. For example, ₹150 a day is about ₹4,500 a month.

cards.title: Plan yearly costs monthly
cards.text: Festivals, premiums and deposits are predictable. Spread them across the year.
cards.bad: Diwali came out of nowhere again.

cards.text: Five budgeting habits to start this month:

lessons.title: Credit Cards, Loans and Buy-Now-Pay-Later Traps
lessons.summary: Use credit cards, EMIs and buy-now-pay-later without falling into expensive debt. You will learn why paying only the minimum due is costly, what affects your credit score and how to check the true cost of an EMI.

sections.heading: The minimum-due trap
sections.body:
A credit card bill shows two numbers: the total amount due and a much smaller minimum amount due, often around 5% of the bill. Paying the minimum keeps your account in good standing and avoids a late fee, but it does not avoid interest.

For example, say your bill is ₹40,000 and the minimum due is ₹2,000. If you pay only ₹2,000, the remaining ₹38,000 carries forward. At an example rate of 3% a month, interest on ₹38,000 is about ₹1,140 for one month alone. In practice it can be more, because many cards charge interest from each purchase date, add taxes on the charges, and stop giving you an interest-free period on new purchases while a balance is outstanding.

A rate like 3% a month sounds small, but it is 36% a year before compounding, and over 42% a year once it compounds. Few investments reliably beat that, so clearing card debt is usually the best use of spare money.
do: Pay the total amount due every month
Set an auto-debit for the full bill
dont: Treat the minimum due as the real bill
Withdraw cash on a credit card

sections.heading: Your credit score in plain words
sections.body:
Your credit score is a number, usually between 300 and 900 in India, that credit bureaus calculate from your borrowing history. Lenders use it to decide whether to lend to you and on what terms. Some employers and landlords may also look at credit reports.

The biggest factor is paying on time, every time: one missed EMI or card payment can pull the score down and stays on your report. Another is how much of your available credit you use. A commonly used guide is to keep card usage under about 30% of your limit. Applying for many loans or cards in a short time can also count against you.

You can check your credit report for free from the credit bureaus at regular intervals. Do it once a year at least, and look for loans or cards you do not recognise, which could signal fraud.
do: Pay every EMI and bill on or before the due date
Check your credit report at least once a year
dont: Apply for several cards or loans at once
Max out your card limit every month

sections.heading: Know the true cost of an EMI
sections.body:
EMIs make big purchases feel small, which is exactly why they need a second look. Before you agree, ask three questions: what is the total I will pay, what is the interest rate, and are there processing fees or other charges?

For example, a ₹60,000 phone on a 24-month loan at 12% a year has an EMI of about ₹2,824. Over two years you pay about ₹67,786, so roughly ₹7,786 goes to interest, before any processing fee. That may still be your choice, but now it is an informed one.

"No-cost EMI" offers usually mean the interest is covered by a discount or built into the price, and there may still be a processing fee or taxes. Compare the total payable with the upfront price. Also count every EMI you already pay: as a rough guide, many people try to keep total EMIs well under a third of take-home pay so a bad month does not become a crisis.
do: Compare total payable with the upfront price
Add up all your EMIs before taking another
dont: Judge a loan only by the size of the EMI
Assume "no-cost" means no charges at all

sections.heading: Buy-now-pay-later and instant loans
sections.body:
Buy-now-pay-later options at checkout feel like a convenience, not a loan, but most are credit. Missing a payment can lead to late fees and may be reported to credit bureaus, hurting your score just like a missed card payment.

The real risk is stacking. A ₹1,500 BNPL here, a ₹3,000 pay-later there, a phone on EMI and a credit card balance can together take a big bite out of next month's salary before it arrives. If you use BNPL, keep a written list of every due date and amount.

Be extra careful with instant loan apps that ask for access to your contacts and photos or promise money without any checks. Borrow only from lenders regulated by the RBI or their disclosed partners, read the total cost, and walk away from anyone who pressures you.
do: List every BNPL due date in one place
Borrow only from regulated lenders
dont: Use BNPL for small everyday wants
Give a loan app access to your contacts

takeaways: Pay the total amount due; the minimum due still attracts interest.
Pay every bill and EMI on time to protect your credit score.
Keep card usage low compared with your limit.
Check an EMI's total cost, interest and fees, not just its size.
Treat BNPL as credit and avoid stacking small loans.
quiz: Your card bill is ₹30,000 and the minimum due is ₹1,500. What happens if you pay only ₹1,500?
No interest is charged because you paid on time
Interest is charged on the unpaid part
The bank waives the rest after three months
Your credit limit doubles
The minimum avoids a late fee but not interest on what remains.
For example, at 3% a month, about how much interest does an unpaid ₹20,000 card balance attract in one month?
3% of ₹20,000 is ₹600, and real charges can be higher.
Which habit has the biggest positive effect on a credit score?
Checking your score daily
Holding many credit cards
Using your full limit every month
Paying every bill and EMI on time
Repayment history is the most important factor lenders and bureaus look at.
Your card limit is ₹1,00,000. Using a common 30% guide, what is a comfortable monthly usage?
Up to about ₹30,000
Up to about ₹90,000
The full ₹1,00,000
Nothing, cards should never be used
Low usage relative to the limit is generally viewed better.
A ₹60,000 purchase, for example, costs ₹2,824 a month for 24 months. What is the total payable?
About ₹60,000
About ₹67,776
About ₹62,824
About ₹70,800
₹2,824 × 24 = ₹67,776, which includes about ₹7,776 of interest.
A "no-cost EMI" offer appears at checkout. What should you check first?
Only whether the EMI fits this month's budget
Whether your friends have used it
The colour options available
The total payable versus the upfront price
No-cost offers can still include processing fees or a higher price.
You have three BNPL dues, a phone EMI and a card balance. What is the best first step?
List every amount and due date in one place
Take a new personal loan to clear them all at once and forget about it
Ignore the smaller ones
Open another BNPL account
Seeing the full picture is necessary before you can prioritise or cut back.
Which statement about BNPL is accurate?
It is not a form of credit
It never affects your credit score
Missed dues can hurt your credit score
It is always cheaper than paying upfront
Most BNPL products are credit and carry similar consequences to other loans.
A loan app offers ₹10,000 in five minutes but asks for access to your contacts and gallery. What should you do?
Grant access, since it is only for verification
Decline and use a regulated lender
Use it once and uninstall it
Share a friend's details instead
Excessive permissions are a warning sign of predatory apps that may misuse your data.
You have ₹15,000 spare and a ₹15,000 card balance at a high interest rate. What is usually wise?
Clear the card balance first
Invest the ₹15,000 and pay the minimum due
Spend it on a gadget and pay later
Take another loan to invest more
Card interest is very high, so clearing it usually beats most other uses of spare money.

scenarios.title: The festival card bill
scenarios.situation: After Diwali shopping, your card bill is ₹48,000. Your in-hand salary is ₹45,000 and you have ₹20,000 in savings. The app suggests paying the ₹2,400 minimum due.

options.text: Pay as much as possible now, using part of your savings, and clear the rest next month while pausing new card spending.
options.feedback: It cuts expensive interest quickly and stops the balance growing.

options.text: Pay the minimum due and clear the rest slowly over a year.
options.feedback: The remaining balance keeps attracting high interest, so the shopping ends up costing much more.

options.text: Convert the bill into a card EMI after checking its interest and fees.
options.feedback: It can be cheaper than revolving the balance, but it still costs interest and should be compared first.

scenarios.title: The upgrade
scenarios.situation: Your phone works fine, but a new model is available at ₹80,000 on a no-cost EMI of about ₹6,667 for 12 months. You already pay a ₹4,000 bike EMI and take home ₹40,000.

options.text: Take the EMI, since there is no interest.
options.feedback: Even if truly interest-free, total EMIs would take over a quarter of your pay for a want.

options.text: Save for a few months and decide later, perhaps on a cheaper model.
options.feedback: It protects your monthly cash flow and turns an impulse into a planned choice.

options.text: Check the fine print for processing fees and taxes before deciding.
options.feedback: Checking costs is wise, but the bigger question is whether another EMI fits your budget at all.

scenarios.title: A friend's request
scenarios.situation: A close friend asks to use your credit card for a ₹25,000 purchase and promises to pay you back over three months. Your limit is ₹50,000.

options.text: Agree, since friends should help each other.
options.feedback: If they pay late, you carry the interest, the high usage and any hit to your credit score.

options.text: Agree only if they pay you the full amount before the bill's due date.
options.feedback: This limits interest risk, but the debt and the score impact are still yours if plans change.

options.text: Say politely that you keep your card for your own use, and help them think of other options.
options.feedback: The card's debt is legally yours; a kind, clear no protects both the friendship and your credit.

options.text: Lend them cash from your emergency fund instead.
options.feedback: This leaves you without a cushion for your own emergencies.

cards.title: Credit without the trap
cards.text: Cards, EMIs and pay-later are useful tools, and expensive traps. Learn the minimum-due trap, what moves your credit score and how to see an EMI's real cost.

cards.title: The minimum due is not the bill
cards.text: For example: bill ₹40,000, minimum ₹2,000. Pay only that and ₹38,000 carries forward. At an example 3% a month, that's about ₹1,140 in interest.
cards.bad: I paid the minimum, so I'm fine.
cards.good: I pay the total amount due, by auto-debit.

cards.title: 3% a month is not small
cards.text: An example rate of 3% a month is 36% a year before compounding, and over 42% once it compounds. Clearing card debt usually beats any other use of spare money.

cards.title: Protect your credit score
cards.text: Scores usually run from 300 to 900. Tap the habits you already follow.
items: Pay every bill and EMI on time
Keep card use under about 30% of the limit
Avoid applying for many loans at once
Check your credit report at least yearly

cards.title: Look past the EMI size
cards.text: For example, a ₹60,000 phone at 12% for 24 months: EMI about ₹2,824, total about ₹67,786.
cards.good: That's about ₹7,786 in interest, plus any fees. Is it worth it?

cards.title: BNPL is still a loan
cards.text: Missed pay-later dues can bring fees and may hit your credit score. Small loans stack up fast.
cards.bad: It's just ₹1,500 pay-later. Not real debt.
cards.good: I list every pay-later due in one place before adding another.

cards.title: Red flags in loan apps
cards.text: Walk away if an app wants your contacts or gallery, skips all checks or pressures you. Borrow only from RBI-regulated lenders or their disclosed partners.

cards.title: You've got it!
cards.text: Five rules for using credit safely:

lessons.title: Investing Basics: Compounding, Risk and Time
lessons.summary: Understand the core ideas behind investing: compounding, inflation, risk versus return, diversification and time horizon. You will learn to judge claims critically and see why starting early and investing regularly matter.

sections.heading: Why money needs to grow: inflation
sections.body:
Prices tend to rise over time. This is inflation, and it quietly reduces what your money can buy. For example, if prices rise by 6% a year, something that costs ₹100 today would cost about ₹179 in ten years.

So money that sits idle for long periods loses buying power, even though the number in your account stays the same. That is the main reason people invest money they will not need for many years: to try to grow it faster than prices rise.

This does not mean all savings must be invested. Your emergency fund and money for near-term needs belong somewhere stable. Investing is for goals that are several years away, after the basics such as clearing expensive debt are in place.
do: Separate short-term money from long-term money
Clear high-interest debt before investing
dont: Assume money in an account keeps its value over decades

sections.heading: Compounding: growth on growth
sections.body:
Compounding means your returns start earning returns of their own. Purely for illustration, assume ₹1,00,000 grows at a steady 8% a year. After 10 years it would be about ₹2,15,892; after 20 years about ₹4,66,096; after 30 years about ₹10,06,266. The growth in the last ten years is bigger than in the first twenty, because the base keeps getting larger.

A quick shortcut is the rule of 72: divide 72 by the yearly growth rate to estimate how many years money takes to double. At an example 8%, that is about nine years.

Time matters more than most people expect. For example, assume ₹5,000 a month invested at a steady 8% a year. Starting at 25 and stopping at 60, you invest ₹21 lakh and end with roughly ₹1.15 crore. Starting at 35, you invest ₹15 lakh and end with roughly ₹48 lakh. These are illustrations only: real returns are never steady, can be negative, and are not promised by anyone honest.
do: Start early, even with small amounts
Label every growth number you see as an assumption
dont: Treat an example rate as a promise

sections.heading: Risk and return go together
sections.body:
Every investment involves a trade-off. Options that aim for higher returns usually come with bigger ups and downs in value, and sometimes losses. Options that are more stable usually aim for lower returns. There is no option that is high-return, low-risk and always available at short notice.

Risk is not only about losing money. It also includes the chance that your money is not available when you need it, or that it grows more slowly than inflation.

Be very wary of anyone who claims high returns with no risk, or who calls an investment guaranteed when it is linked to markets. In India, investment advisers must be registered with SEBI, and genuine professionals talk about risks as clearly as they talk about returns.
do: Ask what could go wrong before asking about returns
Check that anyone advising you is SEBI-registered
dont: Believe claims of high returns with no risk

sections.heading: Diversification, time horizon and regular investing
sections.body:
Diversification means not putting all your money in one place. Spreading money across different types of assets, sectors and issuers reduces the damage if any single one does badly. It does not remove risk, but it smooths the ride.

Time horizon is how long until you need the money. Money for a goal two years away usually needs more stability; money for a goal twenty years away can generally ride out more ups and downs, because there is time to recover from falls. Matching the investment to the goal's timeline is one of the most important decisions.

A systematic investment plan, or SIP, is a method rather than a product: you invest a fixed amount at regular intervals, often monthly. It builds discipline and means you buy at different prices over time instead of trying to time the market. Before choosing where to invest, read the official documents, understand the costs, and consider talking to a SEBI-registered investment adviser.
do: Match each investment to the goal's time horizon
Read official documents and understand costs
dont: Put all your money into one stock or one idea
Stop investing in panic after a short fall

takeaways: Inflation reduces what idle money can buy over time.
Compounding rewards starting early and staying invested.
Higher potential return comes with higher risk; nothing is high-return and risk-free.
Diversify, and match investments to each goal's time horizon.
A SIP is a method of regular investing, not a product or a promise.
quiz: For example, prices rise 6% a year. What is roughly true of ₹100 kept idle for ten years?
It will buy more than it does today
It will buy about the same
It will buy about what ₹56 buys today
It will roughly double in value, as bank balances grow automatically
At 6% a year, ₹100 has the buying power of about ₹56 in today's money after ten years.
Using the rule of 72, about how long does money take to double at an example 12% a year?
About 6 years
About 12 years
About 9 years
About 3 years
72 ÷ 12 = 6, so roughly six years.
Why does compounding reward starting early?
Early investors get guaranteed returns
Returns earn returns, so time multiplies growth
Banks pay higher interest rates to younger account holders
Taxes do not apply to early investors
The longer the time, the more growth builds on earlier growth.
A message says: "Earn 5% a month, fully guaranteed, zero risk." What does this most likely signal?
A rare opportunity to grab quickly
A normal, safe bank deposit scheme run by a large and trusted lender
A safe government scheme
A red flag, since real investments trade risk for return
Very high returns with no risk is a classic sign of fraud or mis-selling.
Which best describes diversification?
Spreading money so one loss hurts less
Buying many units of one stock at different prices through the year
Moving all money every week
Keeping all savings in cash
Diversification reduces concentration risk but does not remove all risk.
Meera needs money for a flat deposit in 18 months. Which principle matters most?
Chase the highest possible returns
Ignore the time horizon as long as recent returns look good
Keep it relatively stable because the goal is close
Invest it all in one sector she likes
Short time horizons leave little time to recover from falls.
What is a SIP?
A specific fund that promises fixed returns every month to its investors
A method of investing a fixed amount at regular intervals
A type of insurance policy
A loan taken to invest
A SIP is a way of investing, not a product, and it does not guarantee returns.
An illustration shows ₹1,00,000 growing to about ₹4,66,096 in 20 years at 8%. How should you read it?
As a minimum return you are owed
As proof the investment is safe
As the bank's promise
As an example; real results vary
Illustrations show how compounding works, not what any investment will deliver.
The market falls 10% in a month, and your goal is 15 years away. What is generally the most sensible reaction?
Check the plan still fits the goal
Sell everything immediately and wait for the news to improve
Borrow money to invest more
Stop all saving permanently
Long horizons can absorb short-term falls; decisions should follow the plan, not fear.
Before following someone's investment suggestion, what should you check?
How many followers they have online
Their SEBI registration and how they explain risk
Whether they regularly post screenshots of their trading profits
Whether the tip is free
Registration and a clear explanation of risks are basic signs of a genuine professional.

scenarios.title: The tip from a senior
scenarios.situation: A senior at your office says he made a lot of money in one small company's shares and you should put your whole ₹1,50,000 savings into it before it "takes off". That money is also your emergency fund.

options.text: Keep your emergency fund aside and learn about diversification and time horizons before investing any long-term money.
options.feedback: Emergency money should stay stable, and one tip is not a plan.

options.text: Invest half of it in the company and keep half as backup.
options.feedback: It still risks emergency money on a single unverified tip.

options.text: Invest a small amount only to try it out.
options.feedback: Limiting exposure is better, but it is still acting on a tip rather than a plan.

scenarios.title: Too small to matter?
scenarios.situation: You are 24 and can spare ₹2,000 a month after your emergency fund and expenses. A friend says it is too small to bother investing and you should wait until you earn more.

options.text: Agree and wait until you can invest ₹10,000 a month.
options.feedback: Waiting gives up years of compounding and delays the habit.

options.text: Start a regular amount now after learning the basics, and increase it as your income grows.
options.feedback: Time and habit matter more than the starting amount.

options.text: Save the ₹2,000 in your bank account until you decide.
options.feedback: Saving is good, but an open-ended delay can turn into years of inaction.

scenarios.title: The scary month
scenarios.situation: Your regular monthly investment, started a year ago for a goal ten years away, shows a fall of 12% this month. Social media is full of panic posts.

options.text: Stop and withdraw everything to avoid further losses.
options.feedback: Selling in panic can lock in losses that a long horizon might have recovered from.

options.text: Review your goal and time horizon calmly, and continue if the plan still fits.
options.feedback: Decisions based on your goal, not on headlines, are the core of long-term investing.

options.text: Pause for a few months until things look calmer.
options.feedback: Pausing is less damaging than selling, but trying to time the market rarely works.

options.text: Move all your money to whatever went up most this month.
options.feedback: Chasing recent winners ignores risk and diversification.

cards.title: How investing really works
cards.text: No tips, no products, no promises. Just the ideas behind every good decision: inflation, compounding, risk, diversification and time.

cards.title: Inflation shrinks idle money
cards.text: Prices rise over time, so idle money buys less each year.
cards.example: For example, at 6% a year, something costing ₹100 today costs about ₹179 in ten years.

cards.title: Compounding loves time
cards.text: Returns earn returns. Assuming a steady 8% only for illustration, ₹1 lakh becomes about ₹2.16 lakh in 10 years and ₹10.06 lakh in 30. Real returns vary and can be negative.

cards.title: Start small, start early
cards.text: For example, ₹5,000 a month at an assumed steady 8%: from 25 to 60, about ₹1.15 crore. From 35, about ₹48 lakh.
cards.bad: ₹2,000 is too little. I'll start later.
cards.good: I'll start small now and raise it with each hike.

cards.title: Risk and return travel together
cards.text: Higher potential returns come with bigger ups and downs. Nothing honest is high-return and risk-free.
cards.bad: 5% a month, guaranteed, zero risk? Sign me up.
cards.good: What could go wrong? And are you SEBI-registered?

cards.title: Spread it out
cards.text: Diversification limits damage from any one bad bet. Match each investment to how soon you need the money.
cards.bad: All my savings in the one stock my senior likes.
cards.good: Emergency money stays stable. Long-term money is spread out.

cards.title: Before you invest a rupee
cards.text: Tap each one you can say yes to.
items: My emergency fund is in place
Expensive debt is cleared
I know when I'll need this money
I understand the risks and costs
cards.tip: A SIP is a method of regular investing, not a promise of returns.

lessons.title: Money Scams Targeting Students and Freshers
lessons.summary: Recognise the money scams most often aimed at students and freshers, from fake job fees to UPI collect-request fraud. You will learn the warning signs, what never to share, and exactly what to do if you are targeted.

sections.heading: Fake jobs and task scams
sections.body:
Job seekers are prime targets. A message on WhatsApp or a job portal offers an interview or an offer letter, then asks for a "registration fee", "training kit charge" or "security deposit". Genuine employers do not ask candidates to pay for a job, an interview or an offer letter. If the offer arrived without any real interview, treat it as a warning sign.

Task scams are a newer twist. You are offered easy money to like videos, review hotels or rate products. The first few tasks pay small amounts, often ₹100 to ₹300, to build trust. Then you are moved to a Telegram group and asked to "invest" in prepaid tasks for bigger rewards. The balance on your screen grows, but when you try to withdraw, there is always another fee.

A simple rule: if you have to pay money to earn money from a stranger online, stop.
do: Verify jobs on the company's official careers page
Search the recruiter's name and company domain
dont: Pay any fee for an interview, offer letter or training kit
Deposit money to unlock task earnings

sections.heading: Loan apps and "tips" groups
sections.body:
Instant loan apps advertise money in minutes with no documents. Some are predatory: they ask for access to your contacts and photos, charge hidden fees, shorten repayment periods without warning and harass borrowers and their families. If you need to borrow, use lenders regulated by the RBI or their disclosed partners, read the total cost, and never grant contacts or gallery access.

Investment "tips" groups on WhatsApp and Telegram show screenshots of big profits and claim insider knowledge. Members are often pushed to install an unfamiliar trading app or website that shows impressive gains, but withdrawals are blocked or require more deposits. Many of the happy members are part of the scam.

In India, anyone giving investment advice for a fee must be registered with SEBI. A large following, confident language and profit screenshots prove nothing.
do: Check lender and adviser registration on official regulator websites
Leave groups that promise sure-shot profits
dont: Install trading apps shared through chat links
Believe profit screenshots from strangers

sections.heading: OTP, UPI collect requests and screen sharing
sections.body:
Here is the single most useful fact: you never need to enter your UPI PIN or share an OTP to receive money. If someone says "enter your PIN to receive the refund" or sends a collect request labelled as a payment to you, approving it will send money out of your account.

Common scripts include a buyer on a resale site who says they will "send money" via a QR code, a fake customer care number found through a search engine, or a caller claiming your KYC has expired and your account will be blocked today. Some ask you to install a screen-sharing app so they can "help", which lets them watch your OTPs.

Banks and genuine services will not ask for your OTP, PIN, CVV or full card details over a call or chat. When in doubt, hang up and call the number printed on your card or shown on the bank's official website.
do: Get customer care numbers only from official websites or apps
Decline collect requests you did not expect
dont: Share OTP, UPI PIN or CVV with anyone
Install screen-sharing apps at a caller's request

sections.heading: Money mules and what to do if you are targeted
sections.body:
Students are sometimes offered a commission to "lend" their bank account or UPI ID to receive and forward money. This is not a side income. Those accounts are used to move stolen money, and the account holder can face frozen accounts and police action.

If you have lost money or shared details, act fast, because the first hours matter. Call the national cybercrime helpline 1930 and report the incident at cybercrime.gov.in. Call your bank's official helpline to block your card or UPI and report the transaction. Keep screenshots of messages, phone numbers, UPI IDs and transaction references.

Feeling embarrassed is normal, but scammers are skilled professionals and anyone can be targeted. Telling friends and family what happened also helps protect them.
do: Report quickly on 1930 and cybercrime.gov.in
Save screenshots and transaction IDs
dont: Let anyone use your bank account or UPI ID
Stay silent out of embarrassment

takeaways: Genuine employers never charge for interviews, offer letters or training kits.
If you must pay a stranger to earn money online, it is a scam.
You never need a UPI PIN or OTP to receive money.
Check lender and adviser registration; ignore profit screenshots.
If targeted, call 1930, report at cybercrime.gov.in and contact your bank at once.
quiz: A company emails you an offer letter and asks for a ₹2,500 refundable "training kit" fee. What is it most likely?
A standard onboarding step
A job scam
A government requirement
A way to show commitment
Genuine employers do not charge candidates for offer letters or training kits.
Someone sends a UPI collect request saying "Approve to receive your ₹5,000 refund." What happens if you approve and enter your PIN?
You receive ₹5,000
Nothing happens
Money leaves your account
Your bank verifies the refund
Approving a collect request with your PIN sends money; receiving never needs a PIN.
You earned ₹150 for liking videos. Now a Telegram group asks you to deposit ₹3,000 to unlock higher-paying tasks. What should you do?
Deposit a smaller amount first to test it
Ask for a receipt before depositing
Deposit it, since you were paid before
Stop, leave the group and report it
Small early payouts are bait; the deposits are where the scam takes your money.
A caller says your bank KYC has expired and asks you to install a screen-sharing app to fix it. What is best?
Hang up and call the bank's official number
Install the app but cover your screen
Share only your OTP, not your PIN
Ask them to call back tomorrow when you have more time to follow the steps
Banks do not ask you to install screen-sharing apps; verify through official channels.
A WhatsApp group posts daily profit screenshots and invites you to a new trading app. What is the strongest warning sign?
The group has many members
The admin is polite
An unverified app pushed through a chat link
The group posts regular market news in English and Hindi
Unverified apps and unregistered advisers showing profits are typical of investment scams.
A senior offers you ₹5,000 a month to let him use your bank account for "business payments". What is the risk?
None, if he pays on time
It can be used to move stolen money
Only a small tax issue
Your bank will thank you for the activity
This is money muling; the account holder is held responsible.
You just paid ₹8,000 to a fraudster. What should you do first?
Wait a day to see if they return it
Post about it on social media first to warn everyone you know
Message the fraudster asking for a refund
Call 1930 and your bank's official helpline right away
Quick reporting gives the best chance of blocking or tracing the money.
Where should you find a company's customer care number?
On the company's official website or app
In the first search result, whatever the site
In a comment under a social media post
From someone who messages you first
Fake helpline numbers are planted online; use official sources only.
An instant loan app wants access to your contacts and photo gallery. What does this suggest?
The lender is extra careful
It is required by law
It is a warning sign of a predatory app
Your loan will be cheaper
Regulated lenders do not need your contacts or photos; such access is a warning sign.
Which statement about scam victims is most accurate?
Only careless people get scammed
Anyone can be targeted; report quickly
Reporting is pointless
Victims should keep it secret
Scammers are skilled; quick reporting and sharing the story protect you and others.

scenarios.title: The selling-online trap
scenarios.situation: You list your old cycle for ₹6,000 on a resale site. A buyer agrees instantly without seeing it and sends you a QR code, saying "Scan this and enter your PIN to receive the payment."

options.text: Scan the code quickly before the buyer changes their mind.
options.feedback: Scanning and entering your PIN sends money out; you never need a PIN to receive.

options.text: Refuse and tell the buyer you will share your UPI ID for them to send the money, or accept cash on pickup.
options.feedback: Receiving money never needs your PIN; you keep control of the transaction.

options.text: Ask the buyer to call you to explain the process.
options.feedback: Questioning is wise, but a smooth explanation may still persuade you; the PIN rule settles it.

scenarios.title: The dream offer
scenarios.situation: After a campus placement you did not clear, you get a WhatsApp message offering a ₹4.5 lakh role at a well-known company, with no interview, if you pay a ₹3,000 "background verification fee" today.

options.text: Pay it, because the company is well known.
options.feedback: Scammers use famous names; genuine employers do not charge verification fees.

options.text: Check the company's official careers page and contact HR through it; do not pay anything.
options.feedback: Verifying independently avoids both the payment and the fake contact.

options.text: Ask the sender to share their employee ID first.
options.feedback: It shows caution, but scammers can fake IDs easily; independent verification is stronger.

options.text: Forward it to friends so they can apply too.
options.feedback: This spreads the scam to more people.

scenarios.title: Already lost money
scenarios.situation: You realise you approved a fake refund request and ₹12,000 has left your account. It happened fifteen minutes ago, and you feel embarrassed.

options.text: Call 1930 now, call your bank's official helpline to report and block, and file a complaint on cybercrime.gov.in with screenshots.
options.feedback: Speed and evidence give the best chance of stopping the money.

options.text: Call your bank tomorrow when you feel calmer.
options.feedback: Delays make recovery much harder; the first hours matter most.

options.text: Call your bank immediately and plan to report online later.
options.feedback: Contacting the bank fast is right, but also call 1930 so the fraud can be flagged across banks.

cards.title: Scams aimed at you
cards.text: Students and freshers are prime targets for money scams. Learn the common tricks, the one UPI rule that stops most fraud, and what to do in the first hour.

cards.title: Real jobs don't charge fees
cards.text: No genuine employer asks you to pay for an interview, offer letter or training kit.
cards.bad: It's refundable, so paying ₹2,500 is fine.
cards.good: I'll verify this on the company's official careers page. I won't pay.

cards.title: Spot the task scam
cards.text: Easy money for likes and reviews. Small payouts first, then a Telegram group asks you to deposit for bigger tasks. Withdrawals never work.
cards.example: Rule: if you must pay a stranger to earn online, stop.

cards.title: PIN means money out
cards.text: You never need your UPI PIN or an OTP to receive money.
cards.bad: Approve this request to receive your ₹5,000 refund.
cards.good: Receiving never needs a PIN. I'm declining this.

cards.title: Tips groups and loan apps
cards.text: Profit screenshots prove nothing. Advisers must be SEBI-registered. Lenders should be RBI-regulated or their disclosed partners.
cards.bad: Everyone in the group is making money. I'll install their app.
cards.good: Who is registered? I'll check the regulator's website.

cards.title: Never rent out your account
cards.text: A commission to let someone use your bank account or UPI ID is not side income. It is money muling, and the account holder faces freezes and police action.

cards.title: Lost money? Do this now
cards.text: Every hour matters.
items: Call the cybercrime helpline 1930
Call your bank's official number to block
Report at cybercrime.gov.in
Save screenshots and transaction IDs
cards.tip: Feeling embarrassed is normal. Report anyway.

cards.text: Five rules that keep scammers out:

lessons.title: Helping Clients Build Better Money Habits
lessons.summary: Hold useful goal and habit conversations with clients while staying within your role and regulatory responsibilities. You will learn to educate without pushing products, keep conversations suitable and honest, and know when to refer a client to a registered adviser.

sections.heading: Start with goals, not products
sections.body:
Whether you are a relationship manager, a mutual fund distributor or an adviser, the most useful thing you can do early is understand what the client is trying to achieve. A product discussion before that is guesswork and can slide into mis-selling.

Ask open questions: "What would you like this money to do for you in the next few years?", "Is anything coming up, such as a wedding, a course or a home?", "How would you feel if this amount fell by a fifth for a while?" Listen more than you talk, and summarise back: "So the priority is your daughter's college fees in about eight years, and you want the emergency fund sorted first."

Goals give the conversation a purpose and give the client a reason to keep good habits. They also create the record you need to show that anything you later discuss is suitable for that person.
do: Ask open questions about goals and timelines
Summarise what you heard and confirm it
dont: Open with this month's product or campaign
Assume every client has the same goals

sections.heading: Teach habits before transactions
sections.body:
Many clients, especially young earners, need basics before any product: a simple budget, an emergency fund, a plan for card debt and an automated saving step on salary day. Helping them see these clearly builds trust that lasts longer than any single sale.

Use plain language and small, concrete steps. Instead of "You need to improve your asset allocation", try "Let's first set aside three months of expenses somewhere stable, then look at long-term goals." Avoid jargon unless you explain it, and never make a client feel judged for their past choices.

When you use numbers, label them clearly as illustrations: "For example, if we assume a steady rate, this is how compounding works; actual returns will vary and can be negative." Never present past performance as a promise.
do: Explain basics like emergency funds and debt first
Label every illustrative number as an assumption
dont: Use jargon to sound expert
Imply that past returns will repeat

sections.heading: Stay within your role and be transparent
sections.body:
Every role comes with clear limits. A distributor's job, an RM's job and a registered investment adviser's job are different, and regulators expect professionals to act within what their registration permits. If personalised advice is beyond your role, say so and refer the client to a SEBI-registered investment adviser.

Be open about how you are paid. If you earn a commission or fee from a product, disclose it in simple words before the client decides. Clients rarely mind that you are paid; they mind discovering it later.

Suitability comes first: a product should match the client's goal, time horizon, risk comfort and understanding. If a target or campaign pushes something that does not fit, the honest answer is not to offer it. Document what was discussed and the reason for any recommendation.
do: Disclose your commission or fee before the client decides
Refer to a registered adviser when advice is beyond your role
dont: Push a product to meet a target
Promise or hint at guaranteed returns

sections.heading: Support clients when markets get bumpy
sections.body:
Good habits are tested when markets fall. Clients may call wanting to stop everything after a bad month. Your role is not to predict the market but to bring the conversation back to their goals and time horizon.

For example: "Your plan was built for a goal twelve years away, and we discussed that values would go up and down. Has anything changed in your goals or your need for this money?" If their situation has changed, the plan may genuinely need to change, and that is a fair outcome.

Schedule regular reviews, perhaps once or twice a year, and keep them focused on habits and goals: Is the emergency fund intact? Have savings kept pace with income? Are there new debts? These conversations keep you useful without turning every meeting into a sales call.
do: Bring panicked clients back to their goals
Hold regular habit-and-goal reviews
dont: Predict where the market is heading
Treat every review as a sales opportunity

takeaways: Begin with the client's goals, timelines and comfort with risk.
Teach budgeting, emergency funds and debt basics before discussing products.
Stay within your role and refer to a SEBI-registered adviser when needed.
Disclose how you are paid and put suitability before targets.
Never promise returns; label illustrations and focus on goals in volatile markets.
quiz: A new client, 26, says "Tell me where to invest." What should you do first?
Recommend this month's featured product
Ask about goals, savings and debts
Show last year's best performers
Suggest they copy what their friends invest in
Understanding goals and basics comes before any product discussion.
Which phrase best keeps an illustration compliant?
"You will easily get 12% every year."
"This fund never loses money."
"For example only; actual returns vary."
"Last year's return is what you can expect."
Labelling assumptions and stating that returns vary avoids implying a promise.
A client asks for detailed personalised advice that goes beyond what your role permits. What is best?
Give the advice informally over a call so the client is not disappointed or lost
Avoid the topic and change the subject
Tell them advice is not important
Explain your limits and refer them to a SEBI-registered adviser
Acting within your role and referring appropriately protects the client and you.
When should you tell a client that you earn a commission on a product?
Before they decide, in simple words
Only if they specifically ask about it
After the transaction is complete
Never, since it is confidential
Clear upfront disclosure lets the client make an informed decision.
Your branch has a monthly target for a product that does not fit a client's short-term goal. What should you do?
Offer it anyway, since targets matter
Offer it but downplay the risks
Skip it and discuss suitable options
Ask the client to buy it as a favour
Suitability comes before targets; mis-selling harms clients and trust.
A young client has ₹60,000 of card debt and wants to start investing. What is a helpful first conversation?
Why clearing costly card debt usually comes first
Which sector is hot this year
How to take a loan to invest more
Why debt does not matter for young people
Clearing expensive debt is usually a foundation for any investing plan.
The market falls sharply and a long-term client wants to stop everything. What is the best response?
Predict a quick recovery to calm them
Agree immediately without discussion
Tell them they are overreacting
Revisit their goal and ask what has changed
Bringing the focus back to goals helps the client decide calmly, without predictions.
Which explanation is clearest for a first-time investor?
"You need to rebalance your asset allocation for optimal risk-adjusted returns."
"First, three months of expenses somewhere stable."
"Trust me, I know what's best."
"Just sign here and I'll handle the rest."
Plain, concrete steps help clients understand and own their decisions.
Why should you document goal conversations and reasons for recommendations?
It shows suitability and helps future reviews
It is only for marketing purposes
It lets you avoid talking to the client again
It replaces the need for disclosure
Records support suitability and make follow-up reviews meaningful.
What should a periodic client review mainly focus on?
Selling one new product each time
Predicting next year's market
Goals, habits and any new debts
Comparing the client with other clients
Reviews built around goals and habits keep advice relevant and trusted.

scenarios.title: The eager fresher
scenarios.situation: Aditya, 23, opens a salary account at your branch. He says his friends are making money in the market and he wants to invest ₹30,000 right away. During the chat he mentions he has no savings apart from this and pays his rent by credit card.

options.text: Explain the value of an emergency fund and clearing card debt first, help him set up a small automatic saving, and offer a goals conversation later.
options.feedback: It addresses his real risks first and builds trust without pushing a product.

options.text: Open an investment in a popular product immediately since he is keen.
options.feedback: This ignores suitability; he has no cushion and is carrying expensive debt.

options.text: Tell him investing is too risky for someone his age.
options.feedback: This is discouraging and inaccurate; the issue is his basics, not his age.

options.text: Share general educational material on investing and suggest he reads it before deciding.
options.feedback: Education helps, but it misses the urgent conversation about debt and an emergency fund.

scenarios.title: The guarantee question
scenarios.situation: A client asks, "Can you guarantee I'll get at least 12% a year if I start a SIP with you?" Your colleague often says "Don't worry, you'll get 12% easily."

options.text: Repeat your colleague's line to keep the client happy.
options.feedback: Implying guaranteed returns on a market-linked investment is misleading and against conduct expectations.

options.text: Explain that market-linked returns cannot be guaranteed, show clearly labelled illustrations with a range of outcomes, and link the choice to their goal and time horizon.
options.feedback: It is honest, educational and keeps the decision about suitability, not promises.

options.text: Say "I can't promise anything" and move on to the paperwork.
options.feedback: It avoids a false promise, but it misses the chance to explain risk and set realistic expectations.

scenarios.title: Target month
scenarios.situation: It is the last week of the quarter and you are short of target. A retired client wants a safe place for money she will need for her grandson's admission in eight months. A high-commission, long-lock-in product would help you hit your target.

options.text: Recommend the high-commission product and mention the lock-in briefly.
options.feedback: It is unsuitable for her timeline and puts your target ahead of her interests.

options.text: Discuss options that match her eight-month need for stability and access, disclosing how you are paid on any of them.
options.feedback: Suitability and transparency come first, whatever the target.

options.text: Tell her to come back next month when your targets reset.
options.feedback: It avoids mis-selling, but delaying a client's real need for your convenience is still not serving her well.

cards.title: Be the professional clients trust
cards.text: Clients remember who helped them get their money basics right. Learn to lead with goals, teach habits, stay within your role and stay calm when markets wobble.

cards.title: Goals before products
cards.text: Ask open questions about goals, timelines and risk comfort. Summarise what you heard.
cards.bad: We have a great product this month. Shall I start it?
cards.good: What would you like this money to do for you in the next few years?

cards.title: Teach the basics first
cards.text: Budget, emergency fund, card debt and automated saving often matter more than any product. Use plain words and small steps.
cards.example: "Let's first set aside three months of expenses somewhere stable."

cards.title: Never promise returns
cards.text: Market-linked returns can't be guaranteed. Label every illustration as an assumption.
cards.good: For example, assuming a steady rate. Actual returns vary and can be negative.

cards.title: Disclose, then let them decide
cards.text: Clients rarely mind that you are paid. They mind finding out later. Suitability beats targets.
cards.bad: There are no charges for you to worry about.
cards.good: I earn a commission on this. Here's how it works before you decide.

cards.title: Know when to refer
cards.text: If personalised advice goes beyond your role or registration, say so plainly and refer the client to a SEBI-registered investment adviser.

cards.title: When markets fall
cards.text: Tap each step for the next panicked call.
items: Listen before responding
Revisit their goal and time horizon
Ask if their situation has changed
Avoid predicting the market
cards.tip: Document the conversation and any change to the plan.
